verses.text: First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone—
for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity.
This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,
who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,
who gave Himself as a ransom for all—the testimony that was given at just the right time.
For this reason I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles. I am telling the truth; I am not lying about anything.
Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension.
Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes,
but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God.
A woman must learn in quietness and full submissiveness.
I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.
For Adam was formed first, and then Eve.
And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression.
Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.

context.author: Paul the apostle (1:1), though some scholars question this
context.genre: Pastoral letter, personal advice from a mentor
context.audience: Timothy, Paul’s younger coworker, left in Ephesus
context.setting: Paul begins the instructions for the church by calling for prayer for all people, including kings, so that believers may live quietly. He states that God wants all to be saved and that there is one mediator, Jesus. He then addresses men and women in worship, a passage written to Ephesus.
context.custom: Ephesus was the city of Artemis, a goddess served by priestesses. Paul’s instructions on women (vv.9-15) have been read in different ways as either a general rule or a response to specific problems of false teaching and disorder.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 3 gives qualifications for overseers and deacons.
context.timelineBible: Verse 13-14 recalls Genesis 2-3 on Adam and Eve. Verse 5 echoes the Shema: “For there is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).
context.sparkNotes: First of all, pray for all people, for kings and those in high positions. God our Savior desires all people to be saved. There is one God and one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. Men should pray lifting holy hands without anger. Women should dress modestly and learn quietly. Paul refers to Adam and Eve, and to childbearing.

overview.summary: Believers pray for all, because God wants all to be saved through one mediator, Christ. Paul gives instructions on conduct in worship for men and women.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes to Timothy, who is working in Ephesus.

history.t: Paul asks first for prayers for all people, including kings and all in authority (2:1-2). Jews prayed for foreign rulers (Jeremiah 29:7; Ezra 6:10), and Josephus says sacrifices for the emperor were offered in the Jerusalem Temple until they were stopped in AD 66. Early Christian writers such as Tertullian say believers prayed for the emperor.

Inscriptions from the cities of Roman Asia, Ephesus among them, name women who held civic and religious titles, paid for buildings and games, and were honored with statues. Wealthy women were visible in public life, which is part of the setting scholars raise for 2:9-15. How it bears on the instructions about teaching and authority in 2:12 is debated.

customs.t: Paul wants men in every place to pray "lifting up holy hands" (2:8). Standing with the hands raised was the usual way to pray among Jews and Greeks (Psalm 28:2; 134:2), and early Christian art shows people praying this way. He adds that the prayer should be free of anger and quarreling.

Paul says women should dress with modesty and self-control, "not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothing" (2:9). First Peter 3:3 gives a similar warning. Writers such as Plutarch also criticize lavish display, and portraits of Roman women of the later 1st century show tall, built-up hairstyles. Paul sets the display against good works (2:10).

archaeology.t: Statues of Artemis of Ephesus show her with rows of rounded shapes on her chest. Ancient and modern writers disagree about what they are: breasts, eggs or other ornaments. Her cult dominated the city (Acts 19:27-28). Some scholars suggest it shaped the problems behind 2:9-15, but the letter never mentions her, so this stays a suggestion.

Inscriptions from the cities of Asia Minor honor women who paid for buildings and public meals. One example is Plancia Magna of Perge, in the 2nd century AD. Most known examples are later than Paul, so they show what was possible in those cities rather than describing the women of the church at Ephesus.

overview.discussion: Paul begins with prayer for rulers and everyone. Whom do I find hardest to pray for, and what would change if I did?
